newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN DLR BOUNCES AS DATA SPOIL BEARS' PICNIC.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN DLR BOUNCES AS DATA SPOIL BEARS' PICNIC.

text.p: The Australian dollar bounced 1/4 cent at the midsession after jobs data failed to meet bearish expectations, so triggering a burst of short covering.

Employment rose 21,300 in July which was just under forecasts of 25,000 but a lot better than the dire result speculative sellers had been looking for. The unemployment rate did nudge up to 8.7 percent from 8.5 percent, but this was more than balanced by a healthy 52,500 jump in full-time jobs.
Analysts reckoned the data held enough promise to temper talk of an easing for now, but cautioned the improvement would have to be sustained for a few months before bulls could relax.

By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar had pawed its way to US$0.7360/65 from US$0.7340/45 just before the data hit dealing screens. But it was only a shade up on Wednesday's US$0.7355/60 finish reflecting the feeling the figures had only temporarily reduced the risk of another official rate cut.

Dealers saw some scope for further short covering near term which could see the currency back to 74 cents but suspected there were far too many offers atop US$0.7420 resistance to allow it any higher. That was a technical recipe for further consolidation with the risk biased to the downside while under the key US$0.7440 level.
The dollar had dipped as deep as US$0.7330 overnight as bears bet the jobs data would dire enough to substantially raise the risk of another policy easing.

Although the actual figures frustrated their ambitions, they were not so strong the chance of a cut had been significantly rediced either. Indeed, analysts noted the July rise in jobs combined with the 11,900 gain in June, still did not make up for May's shock 40,300 drop.
The jump in full-time employment looked more meaningful, but again only compensated for the 63,900 fall recorded in the first six months of the year.
The rise in the unemployment rate, while often ignored by the market, could still have an adverse impact on consumer psychology especially if the media played it up.

Much of the recent softness in the economy has been attributed to consumers being too scared of losing their jobs to spend more money, and an unemployment rate of 8.7 percent weas hardly likely to reassure them on that point.

Analysts expected the sober message to be reinforced by housing finance data on Friday where private banking figures suggest a fall in commitments of around 5.0 percent was likely, even though median estimates were for a 2.0 percent rise.
Such a fall in June would be particularly disappointing since it suggested the rate cut of May 23 had little immediate impact on the housing market.
On the crosses, short covering helped pare the dollar's offshore losses and leave it at 87.33/43 yen from 87.67/77 late here Wednesday.
It was firmer on an ailing mark at 1.3854/71 from 1.3817/34 and steady in trade weighted terms at 57.9.
